body.text: The police commissioner, deputy commissioner and police minister have finished giving their update for today on the death of Constable Mia Lay.
Skip to main content Skip to news navigation, settings and search
A police officer who died after a marked vehicle crashed into a tree in inner-Sydney has been identified as Mia Lay.
The 20-year-old constable was travelling in the passenger seat when the car collided with a tree in Redfern.
A 24-year-old male constable, who police said was driving at the time, has been taken to hospital in a stable condition.
A young officer who died in a crash during a pursuit in inner-Sydney had only been in the force for 16 months and loved her job, police say.
Mia Lay was responding to a car theft in Glebe under lights and sirens about 1:30am along Gibbons Street in Redfern.
The 20-year-old, who was in the passenger seat, died instantly when the marked patrol vehicle she was travelling in collided with a tree.
NSW Ambulance paramedics treated a 24-year-old male constable at the scene, who police said was the driver of the police vehicle.
He was taken to Royal Prince Alfred Hospital in a stable condition.
Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said Lay was attested in May last year and had shown exceptional promise as an officer.
"To lose her, both in her prime, and at the infancy of becoming a police officer is a terrible tragedy," he said.
Commissioner Lanyon said it was "a terribly difficult day" for Lay's loved ones and the broader policing community.
"To Mia, thank you for your courage, thank you for choosing to join the News South Wales Police Force, and thank you for serving the community of New South Wales,"
"You will not be forgotten."
Minister for Police Yasmin Catley said Lay's colleagues described her as an "angel" and that she was destined for a "wonderful career".
She said both her parents described "her love for her job" and how much she loved being a police officer.
"She went to work yesterday and she didn't come home, and that is incredibly sad," Ms Catley said.
"I often say it's a job like no other, but to not come home, to lose one of our precious police is a very, very sad and dark day."
Deputy Commissioner David Hudson said a critical incident investigation was underway.
"It will be a complex investigation but we will get answers out of that and we've assured the family members of that," he said.
Commissioner Lanyon said the crash investigation unit were at the scene to "examine every circumstance" and that police would also examine whether the driver was following standard protocol.
"When officers are actually travelling on urgent duty, when they have lights and sirens on, they are exempt under the Australian road rules, so they can exceed the speed limit," he said.
"But we need to understand the circumstances."
He said there was no set speed limit for police but officers were required to drive according to road conditions, taking into account other vehicles, time and weather.
Local resident Stuart said he heard the crash from his bed.
"We just heard a very, very large crunching, banging sound, almost sort of like gun shots, but it was just once," he said.
"We knew there was something straight away and we looked out, we couldn't see very much but we could see the police lights straight away."
The Police Association of NSW (PANSW) said officers across the state were shocked by the sudden death of their colleague and concerned for the male constable taken to hospital.
"PANSW field organisers have been at the scene, the police station and the hospital since shortly after the crash," it said in a post on social media.
"They are supporting members and families and helping coordinate welfare services."
NSW Premier Chris Minns said his thoughts were with the officer's family, friends and colleagues.
"Every day our police officers put themselves in harm's way to keep the rest of us safe, and today the entire NSW Police family will be grieving," he said in a statement.
NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane said she was heartbroken by the news.
"She was out working while most of us were asleep, protecting the community," she said.
Police established a crime scene and declared the crash a critical incident.
The Law Enforcement Conduct Commission said it had been notified and was independently monitoring the police investigation.
Look back at how ABC readers and other Australians responded to this live moment.
Deputy Commissioner Hudson says it is police remembrance day next week, where Mia will be remembered because she died on-duty.
"We've ensured the family that her loss with not be in vain," he says.
Deputy Commissioner Hudson says Mia has an aunt in the state crime command who was a "mentor" to her.
He says she was too early in her career to specialise but had just returned from a rotation in a different command.
"So she was well known ... more broadly [in] the eastern suburbs area and was a very popular officer amongst her peers."
